AI discoveries in medicine

449 discoveries from 2020 to 2026

About AI discoveries in medicine

This selection contains 449 catalog entries dated 1 Jan 2020 to 17 Nov 2026. 449 include structured evidence annotations describing reported tests, the AI contribution and remaining limits. Missing annotations mean those details have not been structured here, not that a study lacks evidence.

Dates follow the catalog publication policy. Coverage is selected and incomplete; entries can overlap or describe several results. Counts do not measure independent discoveries, clinical benefit or worldwide research output. Read the selection and evidence policy or compare catalog coverage by year and field.

13 Nov 2026Imperial College London; University of Antwerp and Antwerp University Hospital; Maastricht University Medical Center; Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center; Zhongshan Hospital of Fudan University

AI-enhanced electrocardiography for detection and prediction of dilated cardiomyopathy

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: In the journal abstract, an AI-ECG model trained on more than 330,000 ECG–echocardiogram pairs detected the dilated-cardiomyopathy phenotype (AUROC 0.87–0.97) and predicted later disease (C-index 0.80–0.87). In familial cohorts, five-year negative predictive values were 95.5% in Antwerp and 91.5% in Maastricht; positive predictive values were 42.4% and 39.4%. These are diagnostic and risk-prediction findings, not demonstrated clinical benefit.

Technology: Explainable deep learning model applied to electrocardiography

Editorial relevance 53 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
Deep learning model trained to detect and predict the echocardiographic DCM phenotype from ECG; explainable AI-ECG outperformed traditional ECG parameters.
Test and result
Validated in UK Biobank, Zhongshan Hospital and Antwerp cohorts, and in two familial cohorts (Antwerp n=166, Maastricht n=177), compared with traditional ECG features and echocardiographic traits.
Limitation / still unknown
Review limited to the indexed abstract and publication metadata; full-paper methods and additional limitations were not assessed.

11 Nov 2026Google Research

Wearable-based health age models for cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic risk profiling and coaching

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: Google Research reported a wearable-based health-age model associated with subsequent hypertension, cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes in the All of Us cohort (22,748 participants). A companion world model simulated 12-week trajectories. In 490 blinded paired reviews, coaches preferred simulation-grounded plans in 71.4% of evaluations; physicians rated 97.6% of physiological claims accurate. This summary is limited to the November 11, 2026 institutional blog. The authors state all evaluations were offline and retrospective; clinical effectiveness and durable habit change require prospective trials.

Technology: Coachable health-age model, SensorWM action-conditioned world model, feasibility-constrained optimizer with a language model agent, multimodal CKM deviation model

Editorial relevance 53 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Preprint · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
Built the health-age metric and multimodal CKM model from wearable and clinical markers, forecast physiological responses to habit changes with a world model, and filtered and converted simulated habit plans into coaching text with a language model agent.
Test and result
Retrospective clinical-risk modeling and blinded expert comparison of simulated coaching plans.
Limitation / still unknown
Source checking does not establish independent confirmation. Review date: 2026-11-15.

11 Nov 2026University of Florida

MRI radiomics supports individualized Duchenne disease-trajectory reconstruction

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: XGBoost combined baseline MRI radiomics and clinical features to estimate muscle fat-fraction trajectory parameters in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. The final dataset included 98 unique participants, with 68 soleus and 64 vastus-lateralis analyses; held-out reconstructed trajectories had reported mean absolute errors of 0.04 and 0.06. Targets came from a previously fitted nonlinear mixed-effects model, rather than directly observed trajectory parameters. The retrospective analysis identified candidate progression subgroups but did not establish treatment response, prospective prediction or external generalizability.

Technology: XGBoost; MRI radiomics

Editorial relevance 40 medicine Original source Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
Participant-level 80:20 train/test split; XGBoost estimates NLME-derived trajectory descriptors from baseline radiomic/clinical features; reconstruction compared with observed fat fraction. Derived targets can shrink sparse subject trajectories; this is not new prospective clinical utility.
Test and result
Held-out participant trajectory reconstruction compared with observed longitudinal fat fractions.
Limitation / still unknown
Independent cohort validation, robustness of derived targets and benefits for clinical trial design remain unestablished.

10 Nov 2026Xuzhou Medical University

TGFBIp expression adds prognostic information in an ovarian-cancer ML study

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: In a retrospective tissue-microarray cohort of 155 epithelial ovarian-cancer patients, support vector machine and random forest models combined clinicopathological features with tumor and stromal TGFBIp expression. Adding both expression compartments improved held-out vital-status discrimination by a reported AUC difference of 0.038 (95% CI 0.002–0.092). Validation was internal, follow-up duration varied, and binary endpoints did not model event timing or censoring. Recurrence specificity and calibration were limited, and clinical utility remains unproven.

Technology: Support vector machine; random forest

Editorial relevance 40 medicine Original source Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
Twelve algorithms compared across four expression-inclusion strategies; preprocessing/tuning/model selection limited to training data, 155-patient retrospective cohort and held-out final evaluation. Specific biomarker incremental-value result, not a clinical-benefit claim.
Test and result
Internal held-out prediction and paired-bootstrap incremental-value comparison.
Limitation / still unknown
External validation, time-to-event performance, treatment confounding and clinical benefit remain unestablished.

5 Nov 2026Balgrist University Hospital; University of Zurich; Polytechnique Montréal

Automated spinal-lesion measurements retain an association with neurological recovery

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: Deep-learning segmentation enabled automatic MRI lesion measurements in 83 spinal-cord injury patients from eight sites. In the observed cohort, lesion width and preserved tissue bridges separated groups with different six-month recovery profiles. These are exploratory within-cohort associations, with no independently validated patient-level prognostic rule or treatment effect.

Technology: SCIsegV2 deep-learning segmentation; conditional-inference tree stratification

Editorial relevance 40 medicine Original source Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
SCIsegV2 learned image segmentation supplied lesion and spinal-cord masks for automatic morphometrics; learned conditional-inference trees then identified imaging-defined subgroups associated with observed neurological outcomes.
Test and result
Retrospective eight-site study of 83 patients with clinical MRI and longitudinal neurological assessments. SCIsegV2 automatically segmented lesion and cord masks; geometric processing produced lesion length, width and tissue-bridge measures. Automatic/manual measures correlated at rho 0.540–0.821. Conditional-inference trees fit to 75 six-month outcomes selected lesion width and, for motor subgroups, tissue-bridge width; subsequent longitudinal models described different observed recovery profiles.
Limitation / still unknown
Outcome-derived thresholds and trajectory comparisons use the same cohort, not an untouched external prognostic test. Segmentation errors, partial-volume effects and imaging timing affect very small bridge estimates. Overlap with prior segmenter development was not independently reconciled; no held-out segmentation validation is claimed. Missing outcomes and heterogeneous care/rehabilitation may confound associations. The study does not establish causal tissue mechanisms, deployable cut-offs or improved treatment.

5 Nov 2026University of Shanghai for Science and Technology; Shanghai University of Medicine and Health Sciences; Fudan University; Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine; Shanghai Institute of Technology

Learned ultrasound analysis identifies heel-texture differences between clinical groups

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: Learned segmentation and texture classifiers identified heel-pad ultrasound differences between 76 participants with diabetes and 47 controls. Recurrent wavelet-correlation features contributed to group separation, but the groups also differed in age and sex without adjustment. These are image-level group associations, not diabetes-specific tissue mechanisms or validated patient-level diagnosis.

Technology: H-SAM segmentation with LoRA; XGBoost and other classifiers; SHAP interpretation

Editorial relevance 40 medicine Original source Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
H-SAM learned segmentation produced layer masks; learned classifiers and feature-attribution analyses identified texture descriptors that consistently separated the sampled clinical groups.
Test and result
Single-center study of 123 participants and 289 heel-pad ultrasound images. H-SAM segmented two tissue layers; wavelet/texture features underwent training-only statistical screening and grouped feature selection. Seven classifiers shared participant-disjoint partitions. The final XGBoost model evaluated 45 image-derived vectors from 18 held-out participants, with AUC 0.9407. Six features recurred across classifiers; macrochamber wavelet-correlation features showed consistent model contribution patterns.
Limitation / still unknown
Patients were older than controls (median 61 versus 49 years), and sex distributions differed; no adjusted analyses isolated diabetes effects. Multiple image vectors per participant define the reported AUC, not independent participant-level diagnosis. Single device/center, segmentation uncertainty and incomplete diabetes/PAD characterization limit interpretation. No histological, biomechanical or causal tissue mechanism, clinical benefit or independent cohort replication was established.

30 Oct 2026University of Gdansk; Medical University of Gdansk; Gdansk University of Technology; Polish Academy of Sciences; University of Utah; Amsterdam UMC

Leukocyte RNA retention modestly changes platelet-based cancer classification

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: Ten learned classifiers tested whether leukocyte-associated RNA retention affects platelet RNA cancer detection. In a matched 754-sample analysis, training on high-retention samples modestly improved some classifiers; most differences were not significant. Adding the retention score to a full-cohort classifier changed AUC only from 0.9247 to 0.9249, challenging a blanket assumption that this signal should always be removed.

Technology: SVM; LightGBM; XGBoost; random forest and other learned classifiers

Editorial relevance 40 medicine Original source Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
Learned classifiers provided the cancer-detection experiments needed to quantify how differing RNA-retention strata change diagnostic performance; the finding concerns assay signal composition rather than a new general classifier architecture.
Test and result
Analysis combined 2,351 public platelet RNA samples with a marker panel derived from single-cell data from 29 donors. Matching yielded 377 high-retention and 377 low-retention samples, with cancer type balanced but residual collection-center imbalance. Ten classifiers used separate training/validation/test sets across repeated splits and validation-only hyperparameter optimization. SVM mean test AUC was 0.76 when trained on low-retention versus 0.84 on high-retention samples; corresponding LightGBM values were 0.74/0.79 and XGBoost 0.71/0.74. Most other training-retention comparisons were not significant.
Limitation / still unknown
RNA retention score is a compositional proxy, not physical purity or a causal manipulation. Residual collection-center confounding remains; repeated overlapping splits do not provide 30 independent biological replications. Model-specific modest effects do not establish universally beneficial retention, a correction standard or clinical benefit. The full-cohort added-score comparison was nearly null, and generalization to separately collected clinical cohorts is untested.

Editorial relevance 33 medicine Original source Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
DBSCAN learned density structure in longitudinal QA changes and flagged sparse observations, enabling targeted linkage of unusual measured signals to service documentation rather than a fixed list of expected calibration effects.
Test and result
Retrospective 2018–2024 EPID QA measurements and service histories from nine TrueBeam accelerators across six institutions. DBSCAN fit dense/noise groups separately to one-dimensional changes in each machine/metric, with a dataset-specific neighborhood rule. In one machine, 15 jaw-position outliers included a 1.3 mm apparent shift near a documented calibration. Limitation / still unknown
Temporal associations do not establish service causation or independently confirmed physical faults. Apparent jaw shifts after steering may be measurement artifacts. Acquisition timing and detector recalibration records were incomplete, and two machines lacked complete service histories. Clustering parameters were not optimized against prospective truth; noise-versus-cluster statistical comparisons are circular. No sensitivity/specificity, superiority to existing QA, safer treatment or patient benefit was established.

Technology: Latent class mixture learning; latent transition analysis in Mplus

Editorial relevance 40 medicine Original source Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
Probabilistic latent-mixture and transition learning estimated multidomain classes and membership transitions from clinical measurements; these learned representations enabled the reported stability and emergent severe-profile finding. Conventional secondary logistic regression is not the enabling AI claim.
Test and result
Eleven motor, cognitive and psychiatric indicators defined learned latent classes. Mplus latent-transition models compared three- and four-class follow-up structures using likelihood-based fit, information criteria and entropy; the selected model had three baseline and four follow-up classes. Among 250 analytic participants, 190 retained their class over a mean 2.51 years. The severe multidomain follow-up class had dementia in 64%, versus at most 7% in the other classes. Available autopsy information supported exclusion of nine non-Parkinson diagnoses before the analytic cohort was formed.
Limitation / still unknown
Only two assessment times and a predominantly White, non-Hispanic cohort constrain trajectory interpretation. Classes are data-dependent clinical profiles, not validated biological taxonomy. Dementia-related indicators contribute to the learned profiles, so dementia enrichment is not independent diagnostic validation. Same-cohort class transitions and secondary regression associations do not establish causal progression, universal eventual convergence, independent forecasting or treatment benefit.

Target-engagement assays supported transporter inhibition without expression downregulation. In xenografts, Ib18 increased mitoxantrone antitumor activity and tumor accumulation without a detected increase in systemic toxicity.

Editorial relevance 60 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

AI-based generation contributed candidates to a natural-product-inspired library; structure-guided prioritization selected optimized analogues for synthesis and functional tests. The authors tested Ib18 and It12 in transporter-overexpressing cells and evaluated Ib18 with mitoxantrone in xenografts.
Test and result
Target-engagement assays supported transporter inhibition without expression downregulation.
Limitation / still unknown
The evidence is cellular and preclinical xenograft evidence, not patient efficacy or established clinical safety. The abstract reports no systemic toxicity increase in the studied xenograft setting, which should not be generalized. AI contribution

TriNetX retrospective cohort of 61,117 patients receiving checkpoint therapy in 2010–2023, including 1,172 coded cardiac inflammatory events within 90 days. Missing diagnoses/exposures were treated as absent; calibration and rare-event precision were limited. Editorial relevance 47 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

AI contribution
Researchers used five feature-selection algorithms to identify shared predictors and trained/evaluated eight classifiers on routine clinical and laboratory measurements. The selected LightGBM model produced patient-level MIg-positive probabilities; its diagnostic performance was measured against serum immunofixation results in independent multi-center and later-collected cohorts, including direct comparisons with serum protein electrophoresis and nonspecialist clinicians.

In an independent three-hospital cohort of 2,270 patients referred for immunofixation testing, the model achieved an AUC of 0.945, with 87.0% sensitivity and 89.6% specificity.
Limitation / still unknown
This is retrospective diagnostic validation, not evidence that screening with the model improves health outcomes or shortens diagnosis in practice. All participants had been referred for immunofixation testing at tertiary or regional hospitals; an unselected community or primary-care population was not studied. The 627-patient later cohort was time-extended but not strictly prospective. The model is an adjunct for flagging patients for confirmatory tests; immunofixation remained the reference standard, and the paper states broader population validation and clinical utility remain to be established.

In a two-center cohort of 364 participants with type 2 diabetes and controls, targeted serum/urine metabolite measurements found a high-serum/low-urine pattern for indoxyl sulfate and related metabolites in early diabetic kidney disease (DKD), consistent with reduced tubular secretion.
Limitation / still unknown
The external cohort validation was cross-sectional; the paper says longitudinal follow-up for hard kidney outcomes is ongoing. Its projected three-year event rates are theoretical Monte Carlo simulations based on cross-sectional data and are not observed outcomes. The study did not measure proximal-tubule transporter expression or compare directly against KIM-1 or NGAL, and generalization beyond the two Chinese centers and population requires further validation. Metabolite flux supports, but does not prove, tubular transport dysfunction.

11 Feb 2026Cedars-Sinai Medical Center; Valar Labs; Johns Hopkins University; University of Pittsburgh Medical Center; Pancreatic Cancer Action Network; University Health Network / Princess Margaret Cancer Centre

AI-derived histology biomarker stratifies first-line chemotherapy outcomes in advanced pancreatic cancer

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: The CHAI computational-histology platform generated a locked H&E-based biomarker intended to distinguish advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma patients with differential outcomes on fluoropyrimidine-based versus gemcitabine-based chemotherapy. In an independent validation cohort of 299 patients from the prospectively collected COMPASS and Know Your Tumor cohorts, the 173 patients classified F-pref had longer time to next treatment or death (8.6 vs 7.5 months, P=.035) and overall survival (14.4 vs 11.7 months, P=.003) on F- versus G-based therapy. Among 126 G-pref patients, G-based therapy was associated with longer time to next treatment or death (9.6 vs 7.2 months, P=.038), but not significantly different overall survival.

Technology: Computational Histology Artificial Intelligence (CHAI) platform

Editorial relevance 53 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
Deep-learning models segmented H&E biopsy slides and quantified more than 30,000 histomorphologic features. Using the development cohort, the investigators statistically selected and weighted features into a treatment-preference biomarker and locked its threshold before applying it to an independent validation cohort. The platform supplied the image-derived feature measurements used in the biomarker; this is a biomarker-development and validation result, not autonomous treatment assignment.
Test and result
In an independent validation cohort of 299 patients from the prospectively collected COMPASS and Know Your Tumor cohorts, the 173 patients classified F-pref had longer time to next treatment or death (8.6 vs 7.5 months, P=.035) and overall survival (14.4 vs 11.7 months, P=.003) on F- versus G-based therapy. The locked biomarker was applied to assembled data from prospectively collected cohorts; prospective validation of treatment selection is still needed.
Limitation / still unknown
Validation used 299 patients in two prospectively collected but nonrandomized cohorts; treatment assignment was not randomized, and the authors also used propensity weighting and target-trial emulation. The primary endpoint was time to next treatment or death, not progression-free survival. In the biomarker’s G-pref subgroup, the OS comparison was not significant. The authors call for further prospective validation before clinical adoption. An earlier CHAI study concerned adjuvant gemcitabine outcomes in resected disease; this entry is limited to the distinct locked first-line fluoropyrimidine-versus-gemcitabine biomarker and external-cohort results in advanced disease.

Across seven cohorts and five medical centers, targeted metabolomics confirmed six metabolites—imidazoleacetic acid, ergothioneine, N-acetyl-L-methionine, 2-keto-3-deoxy-D-gluconic acid, 1-methylnicotinamide and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate—as a panel for classifying rheumatoid arthritis against healthy controls and osteoarthritis.

A 2025 study added four cohorts to evaluate the seven-protein-marker OncoSeek test, which combines blood protein tumor markers and clinical variables with AI.

Editorial relevance 60 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: prospective or independent check. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
The locked machine-learning classifiers convert the amplified host-response mRNA profile into separate likelihood scores for bacterial infection, viral infection and need for critical-care interventions within seven days. Test and result

Limitation / still unknown
This is prospective diagnostic/prognostic validation of a specific host-response test, not discovery of a causal infection mechanism and not evidence that use of the score improves patient outcomes or antibiotic decisions. Of 1,441 enrolled patients, 1,222 had valid test results; the main diagnostic analysis used 729 consensus-adjudicated patients, and 1,120 were evaluable for prognosis. Clinical adjudication is not a perfect microbiological gold standard, and the study reports lower accuracy when uncertain adjudications are included. Performance and predictive values may vary with local infection prevalence and case mix. This is distinct from the earlier VB10 10-gene signature paper (DOI 10.1016/j.ebiom.2021.103352), which used different genes, cohorts and a different diagnostic score.

Test and result
In a discovery cohort of 43 patients with asymptomatic large-artery atherosclerosis and a validation cohort of 39, investigators combined serum proteomics with machine learning to distinguish acute ischemic stroke from large-artery atherosclerosis.

The abstract reports 43 discovery and 39 validation participants, but does not establish prospective prediction or external clinical deployment. The paper is a distinct 2025 model iteration and validation study in the lineage of the group’s 2022 arXiv proof of concept (10.48550/arXiv.2206.10573); the prior work is cited as antecedent, not treated as a second alias or hidden as the first-ever pathology-image EGFR result.

Cross-condition model-output analysis found that 35 of 37 strongly detectable non-cardiac phenotypes shared signals with only four other disease outputs, and simple ECG measurement models explained some findings.

Technology: PheWASNet, a multi-task deep-learning model based on a one-dimensional EfficientNet architecture

Editorial relevance 53 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
The researchers trained separate deep-learning models on raw 12-lead ECG waveforms linked to EHR diagnoses at two medical centers, then used held-out patient test sets to identify disease phenotypes whose signals were detectable from ECGs. Cross-phenotype prediction comparisons and simple-model analyses were used to characterize shared and interpretable signals.
Test and result
In held-out patient splits at both centers, the study reported previously unrecognized ECG associations for disorders including respiratory failure, neutropenia and menstrual disorders (AUCs 0.86, 0.83 and 0.84 at Stanford, respectively).
Limitation / still unknown
This retrospective EHR-linked study establishes model-detectable associations, not causal physiology, screening benefit or clinical utility. The disease labels are diagnostic codes associated with ECGs within 30 days; results may reflect comorbidity or care context. The authors caution that generalization to other health systems and populations is not assured. Some detectable signals were explained by simple conventional ECG measurements, and the paper does not claim that deep learning is required for every association.

This is retrospective external prognostic validation using specimens and follow-up from a prospectively collected cohort; it is not prospective AI-guided care, a randomized test of biomarker-guided treatment, or evidence that using the score improves outcomes. Only 143 patients had evaluable images and complete covariates, and 88 were evaluable for adverse pathology; it is a single tertiary Swedish center. The model’s earlier development setting involved men receiving radiation in North America, so this tests transport to a different population/treatment context. A 2025 conference abstract describing this cohort is an earlier presentation of the same study, not another record.

4 Feb 2025Tianjin Medical University; collaborating Chinese cancer research and clinical institutions

CHANCE uses tumor genomes to prioritize non-cancer drugs with activity in patient-derived cancer cells

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: CHANCE, a supervised machine-learning model integrating patient-specific coding and non-coding mutations with drug and protein-interaction information, screened 5,197 TCGA/ICGC tumors against 923 FDA-approved non-oncology drugs. For ex-vivo validation, the investigators sequenced tumor cells from seven patients with pancreatic or esophageal cancer and tested CHANCE-prioritized drugs; at least one predicted non-oncology drug showed anticancer activity in tumor cells from five of the seven patients. This is patient-specific cell-assay validation, not a treatment-response study in patients.

Technology: CHANCE, a supervised gradient-boosted-tree model integrating coding/non-coding variants, protein–protein interaction networks, drug targets and drug-response data

Editorial relevance 60 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
Trained on drug-sensitivity measurements from 318 cancer cell lines across 647 drugs, CHANCE maps each patient tumor’s whole-genome mutations to drug-target/pathway features and ranks non-oncology drugs by predicted patient-specific anticancer activity. Investigators used these predictions to select drugs for ex-vivo testing in tumor cells from seven patients; the reported five-patient activity result tests the model’s personalized prioritization.
Test and result
For ex-vivo validation, the investigators sequenced tumor cells from seven patients with pancreatic or esophageal cancer and tested CHANCE-prioritized drugs; at least one predicted non-oncology drug showed anticancer activity in tumor cells from five of the seven patients.
Limitation / still unknown
Only seven patient-derived samples were tested, from pancreatic or esophageal cancers; at least one prioritized non-oncology drug showed activity in five. This was an ex-vivo drug-sensitivity assay, not clinical treatment, and the study does not establish efficacy, safety, dosing or patient benefit. The 5,197-tumor/923-drug screen is computational prediction; only the small patient-derived subset had experimental validation. Drug-response predictions may include drugs represented in training, as the article notes 149 of 923 screened drugs were in the training data.

Retrospective three-center evaluation of 1,076 selected angiography images from 420 patients. It achieved AUC 0.738 in 16,875 internal-validation patients and 0.656 in 15,876 patients from a community hospital; external sensitivity was 47.7% at the selected cutoff. Cancer was uncommon, registry records could miss diagnoses elsewhere, and the one-year follow-up/label timing limits claims about detection at the image date. This retrospective study does not establish effective screening or earlier diagnosis.

Technology: DenseNet-121 convolutional neural network

Editorial relevance 40 medicine Original source Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
A 121-layer DenseNet learns radiographic patterns associated with recorded colorectal-cancer labels and returns a case probability for a single abdominal radiograph.
Test and result
Patient-separated development, tuning and validation cohorts, one randomly selected KUB radiograph per person, and registry/EMR colorectal-cancer labels. The threshold chosen in the tuning set was reused in both validation cohorts; external AUC .656 and sensitivity 47.7% were lower than internal results.
Limitation / still unknown
Prospective screening performance, time gained before diagnosis and clinical benefit remain unestablished. Prior cancer was excluded and one-year follow-up used, but the precise diagnosis-to-image timing is not fully specified. Editorial relevance 60 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: prospective or independent check. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
Trained on more than 3,000 urothelial-cancer slides with molecular test labels, the deep-learning model inferred selected FGFR alteration status from H&E images and returned a likelihood for prescreening before confirmatory molecular testing. The device was prospectively integrated into a non-interventional study workflow; molecular tests remained the reference standard.
Test and result
In a separate 350-slide retrospective validation set, the device achieved 88.7% sensitivity and 31.8% specificity; it was also prospectively integrated into a non-interventional study spanning 89 sites in nine countries.
Limitation / still unknown
The 350-slide retrospective validation set was deliberately enriched (150 FGFR-positive and 200 negative; 43% prevalence), and the device fell slightly short of the prespecified 90% sensitivity target. Prospective real-time workflow validation covered only 17 samples in one month (15 predictions; two quality-control failures); production deployment reported 24 samples, with only 20 receiving molecular testing. The 28.7% test reduction is a simulation assuming 15% prevalence, not an observed clinical outcome. This is prescreening support, not a stand-alone diagnosis or evidence of patient benefit.

Test and result
Single-center prospective paired measurement comparison in 23 intubated patients on pressure-support ventilation. 28 Mar 2024Singapore Eye Research Institute; Singapore National Eye Centre; National University of Singapore; Duke-NUS Medical School

Machine learning links circulating tyrosine and distinct lipid-metabolite features to diabetic kidney disease and retinopathy detection

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: In 2,772 adults with diabetes from Singapore’s population-based SEED study, LASSO and gradient-boosting models screened 220 circulating metabolites and 19 clinical factors for prevalent diabetic kidney disease (DKD) and retinopathy (DR), then were externally assessed in 5,843 UK Biobank participants. Both outcomes shared diabetes duration, insulin use, age and tyrosine as important model features. DKD additionally selected cardiovascular disease history, antihypertensive use, lactate, citrate and the intermediate-density-lipoprotein cholesterol-ester/total-lipid ratio; DR additionally selected HbA1c, glucose, pulse pressure and alanine. External AUCs were 0.791 for DKD and 0.778 for DR, versus 0.691 and 0.760 for conventional adjusted logistic-regression comparators.

Technology: Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator logistic regression and gradient-boosting decision trees applied to metabolomics and clinical risk factors

Editorial relevance 53 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
ML feature selection prioritized a shared set of clinical/metabolic factors and distinct DKD- and DR-associated metabolites, then built detection models externally evaluated in UK Biobank. These models outperformed traditional adjusted logistic-regression comparators in the reported internal and external validation. The scientific result is the disease-specific feature pattern and its validated detection performance, not merely an algorithm benchmark.
Test and result
In 2,772 adults with diabetes from Singapore’s population-based SEED study, LASSO and gradient-boosting models screened 220 circulating metabolites and 19 clinical factors for prevalent diabetic kidney disease (DKD) and retinopathy (DR), then were externally assessed in 5,843 UK Biobank participants.
Limitation / still unknown
The analysis is retrospective and cross-sectional; it classifies prevalent complications and cannot establish temporal prediction or causal effects of tyrosine, lactate, citrate, alanine or lipid features. The Singapore cohort was recruited in 2004–2011 and was multiethnic Asian; about 95% had type 2 diabetes, but the study did not separate diabetes types. UK Biobank definitions and available eye-severity measures differed, and validation of moderate-or-worse DR was not feasible. Performance is modest, particularly external AUC 0.791 DKD/0.778 DR, and does not establish clinical utility.

AI contribution
A learned RF combined the four selected protein measurements into a case-classification rule. Test and result
The discovery study included 33 cases and two matched 33-person control groups. The RF used four selected proteins measured more than ten days before clinical diagnosis, and was then assessed in a separate cohort nominally comprising 20 cases and 20 non-infected controls. The source reports 87% derivation accuracy and 47% in the second cohort, explicitly concluding that the model did not replicate.
Limitation / still unknown
The main paper does not fully specify RF tuning, the person-versus-serum-sample denominator for these accuracy figures, uncertainty intervals or all handling of repeated longitudinal samples. The failed classifier is not evidence of an infection-specific mechanism, actionable screening rule or patient benefit.

Finding: In a proteomic study, researchers measured paired CSF and serum samples in a discovery cohort and used random-forest machine learning to select a 19-protein CSF panel and an eight-protein serum panel to distinguish mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer disease from cognitively normal participants. In small held-out test groups, the CSF panel reached AUC 0.984 and the serum panel AUC 0.881; the CSF panel also distinguished Alzheimer-related MCI from frontotemporal dementia, ALS and Huntington disease in the reported analyses.

Technology: Random-forest machine-learning classifiers on CSF and serum proteomic profiles

Editorial relevance 60 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
Random forests prioritized 19 CSF proteins and eight serum proteins to form disease-specific MCI classifiers after proteomic discovery and targeted validation; the selected panels were evaluated in held-out samples and against other neurodegenerative diseases.
Test and result
In a proteomic study, researchers measured paired CSF and serum samples in a discovery cohort and used random-forest machine learning to select a 19-protein CSF panel and an eight-protein serum panel to distinguish mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer disease from cognitively normal participants.
Limitation / still unknown
The AUC test sets were small (CSF: 9 Alzheimer-related MCI and 21 controls; serum: 8 and 21). The study used separate independent multicenter targeted-proteomics validation for candidate proteins; that does not make the small classifier test cohorts large or establish clinical utility. The serum panel was less effective at distinguishing Alzheimer-related MCI from other neurodegenerative diseases than the CSF panel. These are research panels, not routine tests.

The study used statistical differential-expression testing to select disease-associated candidate proteins, then fitted logistic-regression models to predict MS diagnosis and 2-year disease activity and a linear-regression model to predict long-term normalized age-related MS severity. Stepwise feature selection produced the protein combinations; the frozen models were evaluated in a separate prospective cohort.
Test and result
Using Olink proteomics of 1,463 proteins in CSF and plasma from two prospective Swedish cohorts, the study trained prediction models for multiple-sclerosis diagnosis, 2-year disease activity and long-term disability worsening.
Limitation / still unknown
The study included 143 people with early-stage MS and 43 healthy controls across discovery and replication cohorts; the replication MS cohort had 51 participants. The 2-year disease-activity comparison in replication was especially small (45 with activity versus 5 without). The plasma severity model had only 12 eligible replication samples and performed less convincingly. These are cohort-level results, not a clinically validated diagnostic assay or independent replication by another research group.

3 Jul 2023University of California, Los Angeles; Stanford University; EarlyDiagnostics; University of Southern California; University of California, San Diego

Deep learning detects elevated tissue-derived cfDNA across cancer and cirrhosis cohorts

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: A study built a fragment-level methylation atlas from 521 noncancer tissue samples spanning 29 human tissue types and used it with cfSort, a supervised deep neural network, to estimate tissue composition in plasma cell-free DNA. Applying cfSort to patient data, the investigators found higher cfDNA fractions from the affected tissue in liver, lung, colorectal and stomach cancer and cirrhosis cohorts than in healthy controls; the estimated fractions also increased with cancer stage. The tissue-origin signal was reproduced on an independent whole-genome-bisulfite-sequencing dataset for liver cancer. In serial samples from four non-small-cell lung cancer patients receiving anti-PD-1 therapy, estimated liver or kidney tissue fractions tracked measured biochemical markers of organ injury.

Technology: cfSort, an ensemble of two dense deep neural networks trained on simulated mixtures using a fragment-level tissue methylation atlas

Editorial relevance 53 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
The team used the supervised cfSort model to deconvolve methylation profiles in plasma cfDNA and estimate contributions from 29 tissue types. This enabled the reported comparison of affected-tissue cfDNA fractions in cancer and cirrhosis patient cohorts versus controls and longitudinal tracking of tissue-injury signals during immunotherapy. The atlas and model were also evaluated against simulated mixtures and independent methylation data.
Test and result
Applying cfSort to patient data, the investigators found higher cfDNA fractions from the affected tissue in liver, lung, colorectal and stomach cancer and cirrhosis cohorts than in healthy controls; the estimated fractions also increased with cancer stage.
Limitation / still unknown
The disease cohorts were retrospective and the clinical analyses demonstrate association and measurement feasibility, not prospective diagnostic benefit or improved outcomes. The clinical groups were 21 cirrhosis patients and 201 cancer patients, with 100 healthy controls; cross-platform liver-cancer validation used 24 cases and 32 controls. Anti-PD-1 injury monitoring involved only four NSCLC patients at three timepoints. The authors note that disease-specific methylation markers could improve cancer detection beyond tissue-of-origin fractions.

25 Apr 2023Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai; University of Maryland School of Medicine; Hospital for Special Surgery

Longitudinal EHR machine learning identifies patients who may need autoimmune rheumatic-disease evaluation years earlier

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: A random-forest model trained on longitudinal electronic health records from 161,584 people across two institutions identified records associated with high-specificity autoantibody testing for systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs). The model achieved AUROC 0.93 in internal validation and 0.87 on the external All of Us cohort. In a separate BioMe cohort, model probabilities tracked SARD and other autoimmune diagnoses; records could predict later autoantibody testing and rheumatology encounters up to five years before those events. The study also found higher autoantibody yield among model-prioritized individuals than under the comparison clinical-testing rate.

Technology: Random-forest machine-learning model using longitudinal electronic-health-record diagnoses, medications, laboratory results and vital signs

Editorial relevance 47 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
The model ranked patients by probability of receiving SARD-specific autoantibody testing, using clinical data preceding the test or rheumatology encounter. Investigators evaluated performance in internal validation, the external All of Us cohort and an independent BioMe cohort, and tested whether higher scores tracked diagnosed autoimmune disease and identified later testing or encounters earlier in retrospective records.
Test and result
A random-forest model trained on longitudinal electronic health records from 161,584 people across two institutions identified records associated with high-specificity autoantibody testing for systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs).
Limitation / still unknown
The model predicts clinical suspicion and need for rheumatological testing, not a SARD diagnosis. The study was retrospective and opportunistic; autoantibody testing and rheumatology encounters are imperfect proxies for clinical need, and some diseases were not included in the training target. The authors state prospective studies are needed to determine whether model-guided testing improves care or outcomes. The five-year lead is retrospective prediction of later evaluation events, not proven earlier diagnosis or patient benefit.

In 883 archived infant samples, the study reports that the second-tier approach maintained 100% sensitivity while reducing false positives by 83% for glutaric acidemia type I, 84% for methylmalonic acidemia, 100% for ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency and 51% for very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. Several long-chain acylcarnitine and hydroxy-acylcarnitine isobar features contributed to classification, although their chemical identities were unresolved.

Technology: Random Forest classifier trained on targeted LC–MS/MS metabolite profiles

Editorial relevance 47 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
The classifier modeled multianalyte profiles from true-positive and false-positive screen-positive samples to distinguish the groups for four inherited metabolic disorders. Feature-importance analysis showed that complex profiles, including unresolved long-chain acylcarnitine/hydroxy-acylcarnitine isobars, contributed to classification; the model's second-tier performance was assessed against known case status.
Test and result
In 883 archived infant samples, the study reports that the second-tier approach maintained 100% sensitivity while reducing false positives by 83% for glutaric acidemia type I, 84% for methylmalonic acidemia, 100% for ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency and 51% for very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency.
Limitation / still unknown
This was a proof-of-principle second-tier simulation on residual archived California newborn-screen specimens, not a prospective implementation study. The validation sample was not a fully independent external set, and archived-sample degradation and processing batch effects limited biomarker discovery; some discriminating isobar identities and biological significance remain unknown. The reported sensitivity and false-positive reductions are cohort-specific and do not establish improved health outcomes or routine clinical utility.

Editorial relevance 40 medicine Original source Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
The learned RF combined questionnaire and demographic predictors to classify measured previously unrecognized elevated blood pressure, enabling a specific retrospective clinical-screening validation and its observed sensitivity–specificity trade-off.
Test and result
From 37,110 campaign participants in 2015–2019, the analysis retained 20,206 adults without known or treated hypertension, including 4,192 newly detected cases defined by measured blood pressure. Volunteer participation, complete-case exclusions, self-reported predictors and same-visit blood-pressure labeling limit interpretation. Models/configurations were compared on one internal validation cohort, without independent geographic/temporal replication. Single-visit elevated pressure does not establish future onset or longitudinal clinical diagnosis.

Five were available for AC16 viability assays (three independent experiments, six parallel measurements each); one showed moderate cytotoxicity at high concentration. Artemisinin B was tested in 210 zebrafish larvae across seven groups of 30; one death at 0.5 pg/mL and pericardial edema at 1 pg/mL were reported.
Limitation / still unknown
The seven-candidate list is a computational screening outcome. The reported cell and zebrafish assays do not establish human safety or clinical cardioprotection; transcriptomic markers are indirect endpoints.

The source cohort contained 30 COVID-19 patients and 30 controls, contributing 705 and 990 CT slices respectively. Finding: An international crowdsourced challenge (over 1,100 participants, 126 teams, 44 countries) tested AI on screening mammograms from 144,231 US and 166,578 Swedish examinations. The best single algorithm did not beat radiologists (US AUC 0.858), but an ensemble of top algorithms combined with US radiologists' recall decisions reached AUC 0.942 and 92.0% specificity at the same sensitivity. The study is retrospective, uses challenge data and does not report recall rates.

Technology: Ensemble of crowdsourced deep-learning mammography algorithms combined with radiologist recall

A crowdsourced challenge of 126 teams was tested on 144,231 US and 166,578 Swedish screening examinations, with an ensemble of top algorithms combined with US radiologists' recall decisions compared on AUC and specificity.

The study is retrospective, no single algorithm beat radiologists, the ensemble was evaluated only against US radiologists, and recall rates are not reported.
